question.knowledge_point: Solving a 2x2 System of Equations Using an Inverse Matrix
question.problem:
Which of the following represents the solution to the system of linear equations given below?

$$
{\begin{aligned}5x-2y=1 \\ 8x+3y=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
This system can be written as

$$
[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the solution, we need to calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}].$
This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 3-(-2)\cdot 8}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -8 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{31}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -8 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can now represent the solution to this system, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{31}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -8 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Which of the following represents the solution to the system of linear equations given below?

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2x+2y=1 \\ 2x-3y=-2\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
This system can be written as

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the solution, we need to calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}].$
This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot (-3)-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can now represent the solution to this system, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Which of the following is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation?
question.worked_solution:
To determine which of the following differential equations is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation, we attempt to write each option in the standard form.

A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Let's attempt to write $(\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y}$ in the standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2y+{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is in standard form with  $P(x)=-2$ and $Q(x)={x}^{2}.$ Since the equation is written in standard form, we conclude that it is a first-order linear ODE.

All of the other equations cannot be written in the standard form, and therefore they are not first-order linear ODEs.

question.knowledge_point: Transforming a 2x2 Matrix Into the Identity Matrix Using Row Operations
question.problem:
Which of the following matrices are transformed into the $2\times 2$ identity matrix after applying the row operations ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\,$ and $\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}?$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let's apply the operations to each of the matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne I\,\times  \\ B & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne I\,\times  \\ C & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =I\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$C$ only".

$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix Calculated Using Row Operations
question.problem:
The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${A}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 &  &  \\ 0 & 1 &  & \end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
We write down $A$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${A}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{A}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining the Row Operations Required To Find the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix
question.problem:
The inverse of the matrix $K$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
We write down $K$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $K$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${K}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

question.problem:
The inverse of the matrix $J$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
We write down $J$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $J$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${J}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{J}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & ∗ & ∗ & 2 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 & 0 & ∗ \\ 6 & 2 & -9 & 4 & ∗ \\ 1 & 5 & 2 & 1 & ∗ \\ -1 & 4 & 3 & 10 & ∗\end{aligned}]

$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of a NxN Matrix Using Cofactor Expansion
question.problem:
Calculate the determinant of the matrix
$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 6 & 5 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
We use the cofactor expansion along the first row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & ={d}_{11}{C}_{11}+{d}_{12}{C}_{12}+{d}_{13}{C}_{13}+{d}_{14}{C}_{14} \\  & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+1\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =1{C}_{14} \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & ∗ & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 & ∗ \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & ∗ \\ 6 & 5 & 3 & ∗\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{1+4}|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 6 & 5 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1(0\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}|-4\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 6 & 5\end{aligned}|) \\  & =-(0-4(3\cdot 0-2\cdot 6)+0) \\  & =-48\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Polynomial Forcing
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-{x}^{2}-x-1.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.
question.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $, and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma ,$  we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
(2\alpha x+\beta )+(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-{x}^{2}-x-1
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
\alpha {x}^{2}+(2\alpha +\beta )x+(\beta +\gamma )=-{x}^{2}-x-1
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \beta +\gamma =-1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\beta =1,\gamma =-2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-{x}^{2}+x-2.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}-{x}^{2}+x-2.
$$
